question.keyConcept: During the relative refractory period, the membrane is hyperpolarized (around -80 mV) due to lingering K+ conductance.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: What neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction?
question.explanation: At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine is released by exocytosis from the somatic alpha motor neuron, binds to nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate, and produces an end-plate potential.
question.keyConcept: Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter released at the neuromuscular junction, acting on nicotinic receptors.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: An excitable cell has RMP of -70 mv & a firing level of -50 mv, this cell would be inexcitable when its membrane potential is:
question.explanation: The resting membrane potential depends mainly on K+ leak through leakage channels, which makes the membrane more permeable to K+ than Na+ at rest.
question.keyConcept: A cell with RMP of -90 mV (more negative than firing level of -50 mV) is hyperpolarized and thus inexcitable.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: A cell is most excitable when its resting membrane potential lies closest to threshold. Which of the following membrane potentials indicates the greatest excitability?
question.explanation: Excitability is greatest when the resting membrane potential sits closest to threshold, because only a small further depolarization is then needed to open voltage-gated Na+ channels. Of the values listed, -55 mV is nearest the usual firing level.
question.keyConcept: The closer the resting potential is to threshold, the more excitable the cell.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Threshold level is:
question.explanation: The firing level (threshold) is the membrane potential at which the action potential is initiated by positive feedback opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels.
question.keyConcept: Nerve fibers are classified by diameter, myelination, and conduction velocity (A-alpha to C).
options: The strength of current sufficient to excite a nerve
The length of time a current double rheobase is applied to get a response
The potential difference between 2 electrodes across the cell membrane
the level of membrane potential at which spike potential begins

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Local potential (Characters):
question.explanation: Local potentials are graded, decremental, summable, and do not obey the all-or-none law. They can trigger an action potential if threshold is reached.
question.keyConcept: Local potentials fade with distance because they are not regenerated.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Nerve excitability increased by:
question.explanation: Raising extracellular potassium shrinks the outward potassium gradient, so the resting potential drifts toward the firing level and a smaller stimulus suffices: excitability rises. Hypokalaemia does the reverse, hyperpolarising the membrane away from threshold. Hyponatraemia does not raise excitability either; by reducing inward sodium current it mainly shrinks the amplitude of the action potential.
question.keyConcept: Potassium sets the resting potential and therefore excitability; sodium sets action-potential amplitude.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: About the nerve:
question.explanation: The resting membrane potential is generated mainly by passive K+ diffusion through leak channels, and raising extracellular potassium depolarizes the membrane toward threshold and increases excitability. The amplitude of the action potential depends on the sodium gradient, not on potassium.
question.keyConcept: RMP is largely passive, and hyperkalemia increases excitability.
options: Magnitude of A. potential depends on K+.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Repolarization phase is caused by:
question.explanation: Repolarization results from Na+ channel inactivation and opening of voltage-gated K+ channels, allowing K+ efflux to restore the negative membrane potential.
question.keyConcept: Potassium efflux through voltage-gated channels restores the negative interior.
options: Opening of voltage gated Na+ channels.
Opening of voltage gated K+ channels.
Opening of voltage gated Ca++ channels.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: All of the following about local potential are true except:
question.explanation: Local potentials are amplitude-modulated rather than frequency-modulated: a stronger stimulus produces a larger potential, not a higher firing rate. Frequency modulation is the property of action potentials. Local potentials are otherwise graded, can be summated, spread decrementally, and can be produced by subthreshold stimuli.
question.keyConcept: Local potentials are amplitude-modulated; action potentials are frequency-modulated.
options: Can be triggered by subthreshold stimulus.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Nerve excitability is increased by all except:
question.explanation: Nerve excitability is increased by conditions that depolarize the membrane (hypokalemia) or lower threshold (hypocalcemia), and decreased by conditions that hyperpolarize (hyperkalemia) or stabilize the membrane (hypercalcemia).
question.keyConcept: Hypercalcemia stabilizes the membrane and decreases nerve excitability; hypocalcemia increases excitability.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Concerning the resting membrane potential (R.M.P.):
question.explanation: The resting membrane potential depends mainly on K+ leak through leakage channels, which makes the membrane more permeable to K+ than Na+ at rest.
question.keyConcept: The resting potential sits close to the potassium equilibrium potential.
options: Depends on K+ leak via leakage channels.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: All of the following are true about action potential except:
question.explanation: The action potential is regenerated at each excitable patch of membrane, so it travels at constant amplitude however far it goes, which is to say propagation is non-decremental. Decremental spread is a property of local, subthreshold potentials, which fade as charge leaks away. The other statements are true, since the spike is all-or-none, is triggered once threshold is reached, and is terminated by potassium efflux.
question.keyConcept: Action potentials propagate without decrement because they are regenerated at every step.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Regarding resting membrane potential (RMP), all the following are true EXCEPT:
question.explanation: The resting potential depends on leak channels, which are open all the time, and not on voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels, which are essentially shut at rest and open only during the action potential. Potassium leak dominates, which is why the resting potential lies close to the potassium equilibrium potential, and the Na+/K+ pump maintains the gradients that make this possible.
question.keyConcept: Leak channels set the resting potential, while voltage-gated channels are reserved for the action potential.
options: It can be recorded from all living cells.
The inside of the membrane is negative with respect to outside.
It could be explained (93%) by the selective permeability of the cell membrane.
It is dependent on the presence of voltage gated Na+ and voltage + gated K channels.
Na+-K+ pump maintains and stabilizes its value.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Action potential:
question.explanation: The action potential obeys the all-or-none law, so once threshold is reached its amplitude is fixed and independent of stimulus strength. Depolarization is produced by voltage-gated rather than ligand-gated sodium channels, repolarization by voltage-gated potassium channels, and propagation is active rather than passive.
question.keyConcept: Action potential amplitude is all-or-none; stimulus strength is coded by frequency.
options: Could be triggered by sub-threshold stimulus.
Its amplitude is independent on the strength of the stimulus.
Its depolarization phase occurs due to Na+ influx via ligand gated channels.
Its repolarization phase occurs due to K+ efflux via leak channels.
It is passively propagated to the nerve terminals.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Conduction of the action potential:
question.explanation: Action potential conduction is non-decremental; the signal maintains constant amplitude as it propagates along the axon.
question.keyConcept: Action potential conduction is non-decremental: the signal maintains full amplitude along the axon.
options: In myelinated nerve fibers is from point to point.
In unmyelinated nerve fibers is from node to node.
Is faster in the unmyelinated nerve fiber.
Consumes more energy in the myelinated nerve fiber.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Nerve conduction velocity depressed by all except:
question.explanation: Conduction velocity is increased, not depressed, by myelination, because saltatory conduction lets the impulse jump between nodes of Ranvier. Cooling, pressure, local anesthetics and reduced fiber diameter all slow or block conduction, so myelination is the exception.
question.keyConcept: Myelination speeds conduction; it is the one factor that does not depress velocity.
options: Myelinated nerve more than in non myelinated.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Nerve excitability is decreased in:
question.explanation: Extracellular calcium stabilizes the membrane by raising the threshold for firing, so hypercalcemia decreases excitability. Hypocalcemia lowers the threshold and hyperkalemia depolarizes the membrane toward threshold, and both therefore increase excitability.
question.keyConcept: High Ca2+ stabilizes the membrane; low Ca2+ or high K+ raises excitability.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Nerve repolarization is due to:
question.explanation: Repolarization results from Na+ channel inactivation and opening of voltage-gated K+ channels, allowing K+ efflux to restore the negative membrane potential.
question.keyConcept: Nerve repolarization is driven by increased potassium efflux through voltage-gated K+ channels.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Local potential all are true except:
question.explanation: Local potentials can be summated both temporally and spatially, and this summation is precisely how they reach threshold to trigger an action potential. The claim that they cannot be summated is therefore the exception. They are amplitude-modulated and graded, and they cannot be propagated far because they decay decrementally.
question.keyConcept: Summation is a defining property of local potentials.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Regarding the excitable tissues, all the following are true EXCEPT
question.explanation: Excitable cells maintain a high intracellular potassium concentration and a low intracellular sodium concentration at rest, so the claim that intracellular sodium exceeds potassium is false. The remaining statements about a negative interior, the need for voltage-gated channels, and reduced excitability with hyperpolarization are all correct.
question.keyConcept: At rest K+ is high inside the cell and Na+ is high outside.
options: Have a resting membrane potential such that the inside of the cell is negative with respect to the outside.
Have a higher intracellular concentration of sodium than that of potassium during rest.
Have voltage gated channels that are necessary for the occurrence of action potential.
Undergo transient changes in membrane permeability when the membrane potential decreases.
Become less excitable when their resting membrane potential is increased.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: The term chronaxie refers to:
question.explanation: Chronaxie is defined as the shortest time for which a current of twice rheobase intensity must be applied in order to excite the tissue. Rheobase itself is the minimum current strength, expressed as an intensity rather than a time.
question.keyConcept: Chronaxie is a duration measured at twice rheobase intensity.
options: The time needed by a current of double the rheobase intensity to stimulate the nerve.
The time needed by a current of rheobase intensity to stimulate the nerve.
The intensity of threshold current that excite the nerve.
The minimal duration of a stimulus this can excite the nerve.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Regarding the action potential in nerve membrane all are true EXCEPT;
question.explanation: Propagation of the action potential is non-decremental, because each segment of membrane regenerates the full spike rather than passively passing on a fading voltage. The local currents that flow ahead of the impulse do decay with distance, but their only job is to bring the next patch of membrane to threshold, after which that patch produces a full-sized response of its own.
question.keyConcept: Local current spread decays, but the regenerated spike does not, so amplitude stays constant.
options: It is all or none in character.
A threshold stimulus is required for its initiation.
The current is spread by decremental conduction.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: During depolarization phase, Na+ influx occurs via:
question.explanation: During depolarization, voltage-gated Na+ channels open, allowing Na+ influx that drives the membrane potential toward the Na+ equilibrium potential.
question.keyConcept: Nerve fibers are classified by diameter, myelination, and conduction velocity.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: The membrane is more permeable to K+ > Na+.
question.explanation: Potassium permeability exceeds sodium permeability both at rest, where K+ leak channels set the resting potential, and during repolarization, when voltage-gated K+ channels are open. Only during the depolarizing upstroke does sodium permeability transiently dominate.
question.keyConcept: PK exceeds PNa at rest and during repolarization, but not during depolarization.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Impulse conduction:
question.explanation: Impulse conduction is non-decremental: the action potential is actively regenerated at each point along the fiber, so its amplitude does not fall with distance. It is an active energy-requiring process, and node-to-node saltatory transmission occurs in myelinated rather than unmyelinated fibers.
question.keyConcept: Action potentials propagate without decrement, unlike graded potentials.
options: Node to node transmission in unmyelinated.
Point to point transmission in myelinated.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Regarding local potential one is correct:
question.explanation: Local potentials arise at specialized sites such as sensory receptors, where they are termed receptor potentials, and at the postsynaptic membrane and motor end plate. They are graded and spread decrementally over short distances only, unlike the non-decremental long-distance conduction of an action potential.
question.keyConcept: Local potentials originate at receptor and synaptic sites and decay with distance.
options: It occurs at site of receptor.
It spreads by non decremental conduction.
It spreads by long distant signal.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Action potential, all are correct except:
question.explanation: A threshold stimulus is sufficient, since anything at or above threshold produces an identical full-sized response, which is what all-or-none means, and a suprathreshold stimulus adds nothing to amplitude. This is precisely why stimulus intensity has to be encoded by firing frequency and by recruitment of additional fibres rather than by generating bigger spikes.
question.keyConcept: Threshold, not suprathreshold, is required, and above threshold the response is fixed in size.
options: It needs supra threshold stimulus to be excited.
It spreads by long distant signal elicited.
It spreads by non decremental conduction.
Saltatory conduction occurs along myelinated nerves.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: The nerve impulse has the following characteristics EXCEPT:
question.explanation: On an isolated fiber stimulated in the middle, the impulse spreads in both directions, so unidirectional propagation is not an intrinsic property of the nerve impulse and is the exception here. In the intact body conduction appears one-way only because the region just passed is refractory. The impulse is otherwise an active, propagated wave of reversed polarity that carries information.
question.keyConcept: Conduction is bidirectional on an isolated fiber; refractoriness makes it one-way in vivo.
options: Is a wave of reversed polarity.
Is propagated in one direction along the nerve fiber.
Transmits information through the nervous system in the body.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Chronaxie is:
question.explanation: Chronaxie is a measure of time, not of intensity: it is the length of time for which a current of twice rheobase strength must flow to excite the tissue. Rheobase is the minimum current strength, and the firing level is the membrane potential at which the spike begins.
question.keyConcept: Chronaxie is measured in time; rheobase is measured in current strength.
options: The strength of current just sufficient to excite a nerve.
The length of time a current double rheobase is applied to get a response.
the potential difference between two electrodes across the cell membrane,
The level of membrane potential at which spike potential begins.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: The resting membrane potential:
question.explanation: The resting membrane potential depends mainly on K+ leak through leakage channels, which makes the membrane more permeable to K+ than Na+ at rest.
question.keyConcept: Charge separation across the membrane capacitance generates the voltage.
options: Is due to separation of electric charges across the cell membranes.
Is caused by increased permeability to Na+.
Is stable in all the body cells.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: The resting membrane potential of a nerve fiber:
question.explanation: The resting membrane potential depends mainly on K+ leak through leakage channels, which makes the membrane more permeable to K+ than Na+ at rest.
question.keyConcept: Membrane potential is a voltage measured inside relative to outside.
options: Is the potential difference between the outside and inside of the resting membrane.
Is caused by increased permeability to Na+.
Involves the changes in the membrane potential during propagation of nerve impulse.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: The absolute refractory period (ARP):
question.explanation: During the absolute refractory period, Na+ channels are inactivated and no stimulus, regardless of strength, can generate a second action potential.
question.keyConcept: The long cardiac plateau prolongs inexcitability and prevents tetanus.
options: Refers to an increased excitability state.
Corresponds to the last part of the descending limb of action potential.
Is longer in cardiac than in skeletal muscle.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: The resting membrane potential
question.explanation: The resting membrane potential depends mainly on K+ leak through leakage channels, which makes the membrane more permeable to K+ than Na+ at rest.
question.keyConcept: Charge separation across the membrane capacitance generates the voltage.
options: Is due to separation of electric charges across the cell membranes.
Is an absolutely passive process that does not consume energy by the resting cell.
Represents the equilibrium potential of Na+ ions across the membrane.
Is stable in all the body cells.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: The highest number of voltage gated Na+ channels are found in:
question.explanation: Nodes of Ranvier carry by far the densest population of voltage-gated sodium channels, of the order of a thousand or more per square micrometre, because saltatory conduction depends on fully regenerating the impulse at these short bare segments. The axon initial segment is also channel-rich and has the lowest threshold, which is why the spike is normally initiated there, but its density is well below nodal density. Myelin itself is an insulator and is essentially free of channels.
question.keyConcept: Highest sodium-channel density is at the nodes; lowest threshold is at the initial segment. These are two different facts.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Regarding neuromuscular junction
question.explanation: Acetylcholine is the transmitter at the neuromuscular junction. Released from the motor nerve terminal, it binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate and opens a channel permeable to both Na+ and K+, so cation conductance rises rather than falls. Calcium entry occurs presynaptically to trigger release, not in the muscle fibre in response to binding, and acetylcholine is destroyed by cholinesterase in the cleft rather than taken back up.
question.keyConcept: ACh acts on nicotinic end-plate receptors and is destroyed by cholinesterase, not recaptured.
options: Binding of the neurotransmitter to the muscle causes influx of Ca2+
Binding of the neurotransmitter to the muscle decreases the conductance of Na+ and K+ through the membrane
Neurotransmitter is removed from the synaptic cleft by re-uptake

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: As regard conduction of action potential in a nerve:
question.explanation: The thickest myelinated A-alpha fibres conduct at up to about 120 m/s, because myelin forces the impulse to jump between nodes of Ranvier. The alternatives are all reversed: cooling slows conduction rather than speeding it, raised calcium stabilises the membrane and reduces excitability, and conduction is non-decremental because the impulse is fully regenerated at each excitable patch, so amplitude does not fall with distance.
question.keyConcept: Velocity rises with diameter and myelination to about 120 m/s, and conduction never decrements.
options: in thick myelinated nerve fibers can reach up to 120 meter / second.
can be increased by increase calcium.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Continuous conduction:
question.explanation: Continuous conduction is the point-to-point regeneration of the impulse along an unmyelinated axon. Because every segment of membrane must be depolarised in turn, it is relatively slow. Saltatory conduction is the myelinated alternative in which current jumps from node to node, and it is both faster and more economical, since far less membrane has to be depolarised and then pumped back.
question.keyConcept: Unmyelinated axons conduct continuously and slowly; myelin converts this into fast saltatory conduction.
options: occurs by jumping of charges from one node of Ranvier to another.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: About A fibers all are true except:
question.explanation: A fibres are the largest and fastest, conducting at roughly 10 to 120 m/s, and they include the somatic motor fibres. Sensitivity to local anaesthetics runs opposite to conduction speed, because the small unmyelinated C fibres are blocked first and the thick A fibres last. That gradient is why a local anaesthetic abolishes pain before it abolishes touch, pressure and motor power.
question.keyConcept: Local anaesthetics block small fibres before large ones, the reverse of the pressure-block order.
options: They conduct impulses with the greatest velocity (10-120 met./sec)
They are very sensitive to local anesthetic drugs.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Nerve block is produced by all the following except:
question.explanation: Local anaesthetics, severe cooling and sustained deep pressure all interrupt conduction, by blocking sodium channels, slowing gating almost to a standstill, and causing ischaemic and mechanical injury respectively. Myelination does the opposite, since it is precisely what makes rapid saltatory conduction possible, so it facilitates the impulse instead of blocking it.
question.keyConcept: Myelin speeds conduction; anaesthetics, cold and pressure are the classic causes of block.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: As regard neuro-muscular transmission all are true except:
question.explanation: Succinylcholine is a depolarising blocker, not a stimulant of transmission. It activates the nicotinic receptor but, because cholinesterase does not clear it quickly, it holds the end plate depolarised and desensitised so that transmission fails and paralysis results. The genuine features of the junction are one-way conduction, fatigue on high-frequency stimulation as vesicles deplete, and blockade by botulinum toxin, which prevents transmitter release.
question.keyConcept: Succinylcholine causes depolarising block: brief activation followed by sustained paralysis.
options: it shows fatigue due to depletion of acetylcholine vesicles.
occurs from nerve to muscle i.e. one way conduction.
it is stimulated by succinyl choline.
it is blocked by botulinum toxins.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Neuromuscular transmission is blocked by:
question.explanation: Succinylcholine produces a depolarising block by occupying the nicotinic receptor and keeping the end plate depolarised, so the membrane cannot repolarise enough to respond again. Prostigmine does the reverse, inhibiting cholinesterase and enhancing transmission, which is why it is used in myasthenia gravis, and acetylcholine itself is the natural transmitter.
question.keyConcept: Depolarising blockers paralyse by persistent activation; anticholinesterases enhance transmission.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Excitability of nerve fibers:
question.explanation: Local anaesthetics bind the voltage-gated sodium channel from its inner side and prevent it opening, so the fibre cannot generate an action potential at all and excitability is abolished rather than merely reduced. The distractors are all inverted, because cooling reduces excitability, lowering external sodium reduces response amplitude, and lowering calcium actually raises excitability by destabilising the membrane.
question.keyConcept: Local anaesthetics abolish excitability by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels.
options: is decreased by decrease Ca++ ions.
is completely lost by local anesthetic drugs.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Which of the following nerve fibers is most susceptible to hypoxia:
question.explanation: Preganglionic autonomic B fibres are the most vulnerable to oxygen lack, which is why autonomic functions such as vascular tone fail early in hypoxia. Susceptibility ranks differently for each insult, and this is a favourite examination point: hypoxia strikes B fibres first, sustained pressure blocks the largest A fibres first, and local anaesthetics block the smallest C fibres first.
question.keyConcept: Order of vulnerability depends on the insult: hypoxia hits B, pressure hits A, anaesthetics hit C.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Which of the following statements concerning the velocity of action potential propagation is correct?
question.explanation: Conduction velocity rises with both axon diameter and the thickness of the myelin sheath. Thicker myelin means better insulation and lower membrane capacitance, so local currents spread further ahead of the impulse and the distance jumped between nodes is greater. This is precisely why demyelinating disease slows conduction so dramatically even though the axon itself remains intact.
question.keyConcept: Velocity increases with diameter and myelin thickness because both improve passive current spread.
options: Is independent of an axon's diameter
Depends on the thickness of the myelin around the axon
Will be unaffected if the axon becomes demyelinated

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: If a motor nerve has a conduction velocity of 50 m / second how long will it take an action potential to reach a muscle 0.5 m from the spinal cord?
question.explanation: Time equals distance divided by velocity, so 0.5 m travelled at 50 m/s takes 0.01 s, that is 10 ms. Calculations of this kind underlie clinical nerve conduction studies, in which an unexpectedly long latency over a known distance provides objective evidence of demyelination or nerve injury.
question.keyConcept: Latency equals distance divided by conduction velocity, the basis of nerve conduction studies.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Which of the following statements concerning the neuromuscular junction is correct?
question.explanation: The motor nerve terminal releases acetylcholine, which crosses the narrow cleft and binds nicotinic, not muscarinic, receptors on the motor end plate, opening a cation channel and producing the end-plate potential. Noradrenaline is a sympathetic transmitter and has no role here, and curare blocks rather than prolongs transmission by competitively occupying the nicotinic receptor.
question.keyConcept: The NMJ is a one-way cholinergic synapse using nicotinic receptors, competitively blocked by curare.
options: The muscle membrane possesses muscarinic receptors
The motor nerve endings secrete noradrenaline (norepinephrine).
Curare leads to prolongation of neuromuscular transmission
The motor nerve endings secrete acetylcholine

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Which of the following characteristics of an axon is most dependant on its diameter?
question.explanation: Diameter is the single strongest determinant of conduction velocity, because a wider axon has lower internal resistance and lets local current spread further ahead of the impulse. That is why nerve fibres are classified by diameter in the first place, and why the thick A-alpha fibres carrying proprioception and motor commands are the fastest in the body.
question.keyConcept: Wider axons have lower internal resistance, making diameter the chief determinant of velocity.
options: The magnitude of its resting potential
The duration of its refractory period
The conduction velocity of its action potential
The activity of its sodium-potassium pump

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Which part of a neuron has the highest concentration of Na+ channels?
question.explanation: Sodium channels are concentrated at the nodes of Ranvier, the short bare gaps where the axon membrane is exposed between myelin segments. The impulse is fully regenerated at each node while current jumps the insulated internode, which makes saltatory conduction both fast and metabolically cheap, because far less membrane has to be depolarised and then pumped back.
question.keyConcept: Nodal clustering of sodium channels makes saltatory conduction fast and energy-efficient.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Which one of the following nerves has the slowest conduction velocity?
question.explanation: C fibres are the thinnest and are unmyelinated, so they conduct most slowly, at roughly 0.5 to 2 m/s. They carry slow burning pain, temperature and postganglionic autonomic traffic. The contrast with the myelinated A-delta fibres explains the double sensation of injury, in which a fast sharp pain arrives first and a slow dull ache follows.
question.keyConcept: Unmyelinated C fibres are slowest, carrying slow pain, temperature and postganglionic autonomic signals.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Nerve fibers continue to conduct impulses when:
question.explanation: Cooling from 37 to 30 degrees slows the gating kinetics of the sodium and potassium channels, so conduction velocity falls, but the channels still open and impulses still arrive. Replacing extracellular sodium with a cation that cannot cross removes the inward current that generates the upstroke, so no action potential can be produced at all, and cooling toward freezing blocks conduction completely.
question.keyConcept: Mild cooling slows conduction; losing the sodium gradient or severe cooling abolishes it.
options: Extra cellular sodium is replaced by potassium
Extra cellular sodium is replaced by non-diffusible cation
Temperature is lowered from 37 to 30 C
Temperature is lowered below 0C provided freezing does not occur

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Considered as a membrane stabilizer:
question.explanation: A membrane stabiliser is any agent that makes the membrane harder to excite. Local anaesthetics do this by binding voltage-gated sodium channels and preventing them from opening, so no action potential can be generated. The distractors act in the opposite direction, since lowering extracellular calcium and warming both increase excitability, and calcium itself is the natural stabiliser, which is why hypocalcaemia causes tetany.
question.keyConcept: Stabilisers raise the threshold for excitation, and local anaesthetics do so by blocking sodium channels.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Saltatory conduction in neuron is characterized by:
question.explanation: In a myelinated fibre the impulse is regenerated only at the nodes of Ranvier while current jumps the insulated internodes, so the impulse advances in leaps instead of creeping along every patch of membrane. This is faster than continuous conduction and also cheaper, because much less membrane is depolarised and therefore less ion pumping is needed afterwards, making it more rather than less economical.
question.keyConcept: Saltatory conduction is both faster and more energy-efficient than continuous conduction.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Excitability of the nerve is increased by:
question.explanation: Decreased extracellular Ca2+ increases nerve excitability because Ca2+ normally stabilizes the membrane.
question.keyConcept: Low ECF Ca2+ increases excitability by reducing membrane stabilization.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: The site of conduction of impulses in myelinated nerve is:
question.explanation: In a myelinated nerve, excitation occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier, the short bare gaps between myelin segments, where sodium channels are densely clustered. The myelin covering each internode acts as an insulator, so current flows through the axoplasm and jumps from node to node in saltatory fashion.
question.keyConcept: Myelin insulates the internode, so excitation is restricted to the sodium-channel-rich nodes.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: After sitting with one leg crossed under the other for several hours while working on a document at her computer terminal, a 52-year-old woman tries to stand up, but is unable to walk on the crossed leg, and feels tingling and pain. Which of the following explains the loss of motor function without the loss of pain sensation in the peripheral nerves?
question.explanation: Aβ fibers (large myelinated) are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers.
question.keyConcept: Pressure: affects large fibers (Aβ) before small (C).
options: A fibers are more susceptible to local anesthetics than C fibers
Aβ fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers
C fibers are more sensitive to pressure than Aβ fibers
C fibers are more susceptible to hypoxia than B fibers
C fibers have higher conduction velocities than A fibers

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: What type of glial cell provides myelin for the axons in a tract?
question.explanation: A tract is a central nervous system pathway, and central myelin is made by oligodendrocytes, each of which wraps segments of as many as fifty different axons. Schwann cells perform the same job in peripheral nerves but myelinate only one internode of one axon each. That difference explains why peripheral nerves regenerate far better than central tracts.
question.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes myelinate many CNS axons each, while a Schwann cell myelinates one peripheral internode.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: What two types of macromolecules are the main components of myelin?
question.explanation: Myelin is a lipid-rich membrane, about 70 to 85 per cent lipid and 15 to 30 per cent protein, wrapped in many layers around the axon. Its high lipid content is precisely what makes it a good electrical insulator, and that insulation is what permits saltatory conduction. It is formed by oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system and by Schwann cells in the periphery.
question.keyConcept: Myelin's high lipid content provides the insulation that permits saltatory conduction.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Which of the following is probably going to propagate an action potential fastest?
question.explanation: Thick, myelinated axons conduct fastest (large diameter + saltatory conduction).
question.keyConcept: Fastest conduction: thick + myelinated.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: The most important gas maintaining alveolar ventilation is
question.explanation: Carbon dioxide is the dominant chemical drive to breathing. It diffuses readily into cerebrospinal fluid, where it generates hydrogen ions that stimulate the central chemoreceptors of the medulla, so ventilation is regulated minute to minute by arterial PCO2. Oxygen serves only as a backup stimulus through the peripheral chemoreceptors, and it becomes important only when PO2 falls below about 60 mmHg.
question.keyConcept: CO2 acting on central chemoreceptors is the main respiratory drive; hypoxia is a peripheral backup.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Normal swallowing is dependant on the integrity of the
question.explanation: The pharyngeal stage of swallowing is a reflex coordinated by the swallowing centre in the medulla, and both its afferent and efferent limbs travel in the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves. Damage to either produces dysphagia and a serious risk of aspiration, because the larynx is no longer reflexly protected. The trigeminal nerve serves chewing rather than the pharyngeal stage.
question.keyConcept: Swallowing is a medullary reflex carried by cranial nerves IX and X.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Secretion of intrinsic factor occurs in
question.explanation: Parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, which is why destruction of these cells in atrophic gastritis produces achlorhydria and vitamin B12 deficiency together. Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, the inactive precursor that acid converts to the protein-splitting enzyme pepsin.
question.keyConcept: Parietal cells make acid and intrinsic factor; chief cells make pepsinogen.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: When a normally innervated skeletal muscle is stretched the initial response is contraction, with increase in the stretch sudden relaxation occurs because of
question.explanation: Muscle spindles lie in parallel with the muscle fibres and sense length, so the first response to stretch is reflex contraction. Golgi tendon organs lie in series with the tendon and sense tension instead; as stretch and tension mount their Ib afferents fire harder and inhibit the alpha motor neurons through an inhibitory interneuron, producing the sudden give known as the lengthening reaction or clasp-knife response. It is a protective brake against tendon avulsion.
question.keyConcept: Spindles are in parallel, sense length and excite; tendon organs are in series, sense tension and inhibit.
options: inhibition of the discharge from annulospiral endings of afferent nerve fibers
decreased activity of afferent nerve fibers from Golgi tendon organs
increased activity of afferent nerve fibers from Golgi tendon organs

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: In a healthy adult sitting with eyes closed the EEG rhythm observed with electrodes on occipital lobes
question.explanation: In a relaxed adult with the eyes closed, occipital electrodes record the alpha rhythm at 8 to 13 Hz. Opening the eyes or performing mental work replaces it with faster, lower-voltage beta activity, a change called alpha block or desynchronisation. Theta and delta are the slower rhythms of drowsiness and deep sleep, and delta in a waking adult suggests pathology.
question.keyConcept: Alpha means relaxed with eyes closed, and attention desynchronises it to beta.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: Atrial natriuretic peptide brings
question.explanation: Atrial natriuretic peptide is released when the atria are stretched by volume overload, and its role is to shed salt and water. It raises glomerular filtration by dilating the afferent and constricting the efferent arteriole, relaxes mesangial cells to increase filtering surface, and inhibits renin, aldosterone and ADH, so it acts as the physiological antagonist of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
question.keyConcept: ANP is the volume-unloading hormone: it raises GFR and opposes renin, aldosterone and ADH.

chapter: Nerve Fibre Types, Conduction & Neuromuscular Junction
subject: Physiology

question.text: The peripheral nervous system includes the:
question.explanation: The dividing line is anatomical: the brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system, and everything outside them, including the cranial and spinal nerves and their ganglia, forms the peripheral nervous system. The somatic system therefore belongs to the periphery, whereas cranial nerve nuclei are collections of cell bodies inside the brainstem and remain central.
question.keyConcept: Cranial nerve nuclei are central, but the cranial nerves themselves are peripheral.

question.text: Inhibitory neurotransmitters increase the post synaptic conductance due to
question.explanation: Inhibitory transmitters often increase chloride conductance, producing hyperpolarization or stabilization of the postsynaptic membrane and making action-potential generation less likely.
question.keyConcept: IPSPs commonly result from increased Cl− conductance.

question.text: With respect to synapse
question.explanation: GABA is an important neurotransmitter in presynaptic inhibition in the CNS. By contrast, Na+ permeability usually produces excitation, most catecholamine action ends mainly by reuptake rather than cleft metabolism, and postganglionic sympathetic fibers usually release norepinephrine rather than adrenaline.
question.keyConcept: GABA is central to presynaptic inhibition.
options: Inhibitory postsynaptic potentials are due to localized increase in membrane permeability to Na
GABA is one of the neurotransmitters involved in presynaptic inhibition in the CNS
Metabolism of catecholamines at the synaptic cleft is the major method of terminating their action
Adrenaline is the major neurotransmitter at postganglionic sympathetic endings
Habituation is due to a gradual inactivation of Na channels on repeat stimulation

question.text: Which of the following receptors are rapidly adapting sensory receptors?
question.explanation: Rapidly adapting receptors respond strongly to changes in stimulus intensity and are well represented by touch receptors such as Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles. Pain receptors and muscle spindles adapt more slowly.
question.keyConcept: Rapidly adapting receptors signal stimulus change, especially touch.

question.text: The inhibitory postsynaptic potential:
question.explanation: An IPSP is typically a local hyperpolarization caused by increased chloride conductance or sometimes increased potassium conductance. This shifts membrane potential farther from threshold.
question.keyConcept: IPSPs move membrane potential away from threshold.
options: probably occurs only in the brain
is a local depolarization caused by an increase in Ca2+conductance
is a local hyperpolarization caused by a decrease in Ca2+conductance
is a local depolarization caused by an increase in C- conductance
is a local hyperpolarization caused by an increase in Cl- conductance

question.text: In sensory receptors
question.explanation: A sensory receptor converts stimulus energy into a local graded receptor or generator potential. This local depolarization can then trigger action potentials in the afferent nerve if threshold is reached.
question.keyConcept: Sensory transduction converts stimulus energy into a graded receptor potential.
options: Stimulus energy is converted into a local depolarization.
The generator potential is graded and self-propagating.
A generator potential can be produced by only one form of energy.
The frequency of action potentials generated doubles when the strength of the stimulus doubles.
Serving touch sensation, constant suprathreshold stimulation causes action potentials to be generated at a constant rate

question.text: Which of the following statements about synapse is correct?
question.explanation: Electrical synapses can conduct bidirectionally, unlike typical chemical synapses. Most CNS synapses are chemical rather than electrical, and chemical transmission is not the normal mode between cardiac muscle cells.
question.keyConcept: Electrical synapses can be bidirectional.
options: Transmit impulses chemically between cardiac muscle cells.
Most of CNS synapses transmit impulses electrically.
The presynaptic neuron contains specific enzyme for destruction of the transmitter.
In some types, synapses can transmit impulses bidirectional.
CNS synapses are rapidly conducting than smooth muscle synapses.

question.text: Concerning synapses, which of the following is correct?
question.explanation: Postsynaptic membranes contain receptor proteins for neurotransmitters, and a given neuron may express multiple receptor types. Presynaptic terminals are rich in vesicles and mitochondria, and some transmitters can also be taken back up after release.
question.keyConcept: Postsynaptic neurons can carry multiple receptor types.
options: The presynaptic neuron is poor in mitochondria and vesicles.
The synaptic cleft is highly condensed with K+ ions.
The post synaptic neuron has many receptor types for different neurotransmitters.
The presynaptic neuron terminal buttons may release more than a one main transmitter.
The neurotransmitter can never be taken back into presynaptic neuron.

question.text: Compared to electrical synapses, Chemical synapses are:
question.explanation: Chemical synapses are slower and can fatigue more easily because they depend on transmitter synthesis, vesicle release, diffusion, receptor activation, and clearance. Electrical synapses transmit more rapidly through gap junctions.
question.keyConcept: Chemical synapses are slower and more easily fatigued than electrical synapses.
options: Contain connexon that allow the passage of ions.

question.text: In one of body reflexes, the time from application of the stimulus till occurrence of the response was 12 msec., the conduction time in afferent neuron was 3 msec and was double this time in the efferent neuron. In this reflex, the number of synapses and the central delay are:
question.explanation: Total reflex time is 12 ms. Afferent conduction is 3 ms and efferent conduction is double that, 6 ms, leaving 3 ms as central delay. With about 0.5 ms minimum delay per synapse, this implies 6 synapses.
question.keyConcept: Central delay helps estimate synapse number in a reflex arc.

question.text: Regarding sensory receptors:
question.explanation: Most sensory receptors are most sensitive to one adequate stimulus modality, meaning they are activated best by a specific form of energy. This specificity is a basic feature of receptor physiology.
question.keyConcept: Sensory receptors are usually modality-specific.
options: They can only detect changes in external environment.
They respond to stimuli by local non propagated potential changes in receptor membrane.
All receptors adapt to constant stimulation.
They can produce action potential in receptor membrane.
All receptors release transmitters to conduct impulses to afferent neurons.

question.text: Regarding adaptation of receptors:
question.explanation: Adaptation is the progressive decline in receptor potential amplitude and afferent firing during constant stimulation. Receptors differ widely in their rate and mechanism of adaptation.
question.keyConcept: Adaptation means declining receptor response during sustained stimulation.
options: Adaptation depends on the importance of receptors.
Adaptation is the decrease in amplitude of receptor potential and frequency of action potentials discharged in afferent nerves in response to constant stimulation.
Adaptation is the gradual increase in receptor response upon constant stimulation.
The mechanism of adaptation is the same mechanism of fatigue.
All receptors adapt by similar mechanisms.

question.text: Which autonomic receptor is activated by low concentrations of epinephrine released from the adrenal medulla and causes vasodilation?
question.explanation: Low concentrations of circulating epinephrine preferentially stimulate beta-2 receptors, especially in skeletal-muscle vascular beds, causing vasodilation. Alpha-1 effects become more prominent at higher concentrations.
question.keyConcept: Low-dose epinephrine preferentially activates beta-2 receptors.

question.text: Renin is released in response to stimulation of which adrenoreceptor?
question.explanation: Renin release from juxtaglomerular cells is stimulated by beta-1 adrenergic receptors. This links sympathetic activity to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
question.keyConcept: Beta-1 stimulation promotes renin release.

question.text: Nicotinic receptor sites occur at all of the following EXCEPT:
question.explanation: Nicotinic receptors are found in autonomic ganglia, adrenal medulla, skeletal neuromuscular junctions, and on some spinal interneurons such as Renshaw cells. Bronchial smooth muscle responds mainly through muscarinic receptors, not nicotinic ones.
question.keyConcept: Nicotinic receptors are ganglionic and neuromuscular, not bronchial smooth-muscle receptors.
options: Excitatory receptors on Renshaw cell in the spinal cord

question.text: Activation of alpha-1 receptors causes:
question.explanation: Alpha-1 receptor activation contracts radial muscle of the iris and causes mydriasis. It also tends to promote vasoconstriction and sphincter contraction rather than bronchodilation or tachycardia.
question.keyConcept: Alpha-1 activation causes mydriasis and smooth-muscle contraction.

question.text: Which autonomic receptor mediates secretion of epinephrine by the adrenal medulla?
question.explanation: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors on chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, triggering epinephrine secretion.
question.keyConcept: Adrenal medullary secretion is triggered by nicotinic receptors.

question.text: For cells that communicate by electrical synapses, the message travels between cells via?
question.explanation: Electrical synapses transmit through gap junction channels that directly connect adjacent cells. Ions pass from cell to cell without needing neurotransmitter diffusion across a synaptic cleft.
question.keyConcept: Electrical synapses communicate through gap junctions.
options: ions moving across the synaptic cleft
active transport across the synaptic cleft
passive transport across the synaptic cleft .

question.text: Which of the following statements about synapses is FALSE?
question.explanation: Electrical synapses use gap junctions for ion flow, not neurotransmitter movement between cells. That makes the statement about neurotransmitters moving through gap junctions the false one.
question.keyConcept: Electrical synapses pass ions through gap junctions, not neurotransmitters.
options: Communication across electrical synapses is bi-directional.
Neurotransmitters can move from one cell to another through gap junctions at an electrical synapse.
Communication at chemical synapses is slower than at electrical synapses.
Most synapses in the nervous system are chemical synapses. .

question.text: Which of the following statements about electrical synapses is FALSE?
question.explanation: Electrical synapses commonly allow bidirectional communication, so the statement that they provide only unidirectional communication is false. They are built from connexin-based gap junctions.
question.keyConcept: Electrical synapses are often bidirectional.
options: Gap junctions are formed from proteins called connexins.
Electrical synapses connect hypothalamic neurons that release tropic hormones.
Electrical synapses are found in the retina.
Electrical synapses are found in the brainstem.
electrical synapses provide for uni-directional communication.

question.text: The chemical synapse is bounded by the ... neuron, from which neurotransmitters are released across the synaptic cleft, to the ... neuron, where the receptors for that neurotransmitter are located.
question.explanation: A chemical synapse runs from the presynaptic neuron, which releases transmitter, to the postsynaptic neuron, which bears the relevant receptors. These are the two sides of the synaptic cleft.
question.keyConcept: Chemical synapses run from presynaptic to postsynaptic neurons.

question.text: What type of synapse occurs between an axon terminal of one neuron and the cell body of another neuron?
question.explanation: An axon terminal contacting the cell body forms an axosomatic synapse. This type can exert strong influence on postsynaptic excitability because it is close to the spike-trigger zone.
question.keyConcept: Axosomatic synapses contact the neuronal soma.

question.text: The neurotransmitter that is released from the pre synaptic neuron must diffuse across the ... to reach the postsynaptic neuron.
question.explanation: After release, neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft to reach receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. This diffusion contributes to synaptic delay.
question.keyConcept: Neurotransmitters cross the synaptic cleft by diffusion.

question.text: Most neurotransmitters are synthesized in what region of a neuron?
question.explanation: Most small-molecule neurotransmitters are synthesized in the cytosol of the presynaptic terminal and then packaged into vesicles. Peptide transmitters are an important exception because they are synthesized in the cell body.
question.keyConcept: Most small-molecule transmitters are synthesized in cytosol.

question.text: Neurotransmitter release occurs by what mechanism?
question.explanation: Neurotransmitters are released by exocytosis of synaptic vesicles after calcium entry into the presynaptic terminal. This is the defining release mechanism of chemical synapses.
question.keyConcept: Chemical synapses release transmitter by exocytosis.

question.text: The influx of calcium into the axon terminal of a chemical synapse is responsible for which of the following?
question.explanation: Calcium entry triggers vesicle docking and fusion with the presynaptic membrane, producing exocytosis of neurotransmitter. It does not itself initiate the axonal action potential.
question.keyConcept: Presynaptic Ca2+ entry triggers vesicle fusion and exocytosis.
options: fusion of vesicles with the membrane and exocytosis of neurotransmitter
diffusion of the neurotransmitter across the membrane and into the cleft
movement of calcium through gap junctions .

question.text: Neurotransmitters can be reused through the process of ..., where neuro-transmitters are transported across the presynaptic membrane.
question.explanation: Many neurotransmitters are cleared by reuptake into the presynaptic terminal or nearby glia, allowing recycling and helping terminate synaptic action.
question.keyConcept: Reuptake helps terminate and recycle neurotransmitters.

question.text: The extent of neurotransmitter binding to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane is determined primarily by which of the following?
question.explanation: The main determinant of receptor occupancy is transmitter concentration in the synaptic cleft. Higher cleft concentration generally increases the extent of postsynaptic receptor binding.
question.keyConcept: Cleft transmitter concentration largely determines receptor binding.

question.text: The opening of ion channels that is stimulated by the bind ing of a neurotransmitter to its receptor on a neighboring neuron, and the subsequent movement of ions across that membrane, describes the development of which of the following?
question.explanation: Neurotransmitter-gated ion-channel opening in the target neuron produces a postsynaptic potential. Depending on the channels involved, this potential may be excitatory or inhibitory.
question.keyConcept: Neurotransmitter-gated channels generate postsynaptic potentials.

question.text: What is a change in the postsynaptic potential that brings membrane potential closer to threshold called?
question.explanation: A postsynaptic potential that moves membrane voltage closer to threshold is an excitatory postsynaptic potential, or EPSP. EPSPs are graded and can summate.
question.keyConcept: An EPSP moves the postsynaptic membrane toward threshold.

question.text: Presynaptic inhibition depends upon :-
question.explanation: Presynaptic inhibition is commonly mediated by GABA acting on receptors at the presynaptic terminal, which reduces transmitter release from that terminal. This usually occurs at axoaxonic synapses.
question.keyConcept: Presynaptic inhibition depends on GABAergic action at presynaptic terminals.
options: augmented release of chemical transmitter from presynaptic terminals
opening of voltage-gated Ca ++ channels in presynaptic terminals

question.text: Most sensory receptors: -
question.explanation: Most sensory receptors are most sensitive to one adequate stimulus modality, meaning they are activated best by a specific form of energy. This specificity is a basic feature of receptor physiology.
question.keyConcept: Sensory receptors are usually modality-specific.
options: are stimulated by different types of stimuli
are stimulated only by specific stimuli
possess a high threshold for their specific stimuli

question.text: A specific stimulus produces a receptor potential by :-
question.explanation: A receptor potential is usually produced by increased cation entry, especially sodium influx, into the receptor ending. This generates a graded depolarization.
question.keyConcept: Receptor potentials usually arise from increased cation influx.

question.text: Slowly adapting receptors include all the following types, except :-
question.explanation: Meissner corpuscles are rapidly adapting: they fire a brief burst at the onset of touch and then fall silent, which suits them to detecting movement and flutter rather than sustained contact. Slowly adapting receptors keep firing for as long as the stimulus lasts, which is what is needed for variables the brain must monitor continuously, such as pain from free nerve endings, warmth, and muscle tension sensed by Golgi tendon organs.
question.keyConcept: Rapidly adapting receptors report change, while slowly adapting receptors report maintained states.

question.text: Rapidly adapting receptors are involved in :-
question.explanation: Rapidly adapting receptors are especially important for touch and for detecting changes in stimuli. They are less suited for static position or persistent pain signaling.
question.keyConcept: Rapidly adapting receptors are characteristic of touch sensation.

question.text: Receptors detect stimulus intensity by :-
question.explanation: Increasing stimulus intensity usually increases the magnitude of the receptor potential and often the frequency of action potentials in the afferent nerve. This is how receptors encode strength.
question.keyConcept: Stimulus intensity is encoded by larger receptor potentials and higher firing rates.
options: lowering the threshold for stimulating receptors
raising the threshold for stimulating receptors
decreasing the magnitude of receptor potential
raising the magnitude of receptor potential

question.text: Regarding synapses
question.explanation: EPSPs are usually produced by sodium influx through postsynaptic channels. The synaptic cleft is measured in nanometers, calcium entry triggers release, and acetylcholine is stored in vesicles rather than floating freely in the terminal.
question.keyConcept: EPSPs are typically caused by Na+ influx.
options: The synaptic cleft is 30-50 mm wide
Transmitters are released from synaptic knobs secondary to Na trigger
Amount of transmitter released is proportional to Ca efflux
Ach is present freely in synaptic knob
The EPSP is caused by Na influx

question.text: Presynaptic inhibition of the central nervous system affects the firing rate of alpha motor neurons by which of the following mechanisms?
question.explanation: Presynaptic inhibition commonly works by increasing chloride permeability in the presynaptic ending, which reduces transmitter release onto the alpha motor neuron. The effect is exerted before the synapse onto the motor neuron itself.
question.keyConcept: Presynaptic inhibition reduces transmitter release by acting on the presynaptic ending.
options: Increasing the Cl- permeability of the presynaptic nerve ending
Decreasing the K+ permeability of the alpha motor neuron
Decreasing the frequency of action potentials by the presynaptic nerve ending
Hyperpolarizing the membrane postsynaptic potential of the alpha motor neuron
Increasing the amount of neurotransmitter released by the presynaptic nerve ending

question.text: The influx of Ca2+ into the presynaptic terminal during synaptic transmission is due primarily to what?
question.explanation: Depolarization of the presynaptic membrane opens voltage-gated calcium channels, allowing calcium influx. This calcium signal then triggers exocytosis.
question.keyConcept: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open when the presynaptic terminal depolarizes.
options: A neurotransmitter-mediated increase in membrane Ca
Depolarization of membrane potential that increases the driving force for inward Ca2+ current
Opening of voltage-activated Ca2+ channels in the membrane

question.text: Which of the following is an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system (CNS)?
question.explanation: GABA is a principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS. It commonly increases chloride conductance and helps generate inhibitory postsynaptic effects.
question.keyConcept: GABA is a major inhibitory CNS neurotransmitter.

question.text: Excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSP) are not produced by:
question.explanation: Opening chloride channels usually produces inhibition rather than excitation, because it hyperpolarizes or stabilizes the membrane potential. Therefore it does not generate an EPSP.
question.keyConcept: Opening Cl− channels does not produce an EPSP.

question.text: Slow inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSP) may be produced by:
question.explanation: Slow IPSPs can be produced by opening potassium channels, which allows K+ efflux and hyperpolarizes the postsynaptic membrane. Fast IPSPs are more classically linked to chloride channels.
question.keyConcept: Slow IPSPs can result from opening K+ channels.

question.text: The minimum time for transmission across one synapse is:
question.explanation: The minimum synaptic delay across a single chemical synapse is about 0.5 ms. This value is often used to estimate synapse number in reflex pathways.
question.keyConcept: One chemical synapse delays transmission by about 0.5 ms.

question.text: Presynaptic inhibition occurs at:
question.explanation: Presynaptic inhibition classically occurs at axoaxonic synapses, where one axon terminal modulates neurotransmitter release from another.
question.keyConcept: Presynaptic inhibition occurs at axoaxonic synapses.

question.text: The inhibitory amino acid neurotransmitters in the CNS are:
question.explanation: The main inhibitory amino acid neurotransmitters in the CNS are GABA and glycine. Both reduce neuronal excitability through inhibitory synaptic mechanisms.
question.keyConcept: GABA and glycine are the main inhibitory amino acid transmitters in the CNS.

question.text: “No matter where a particular sensory pathway is stimulated along its course to the cortex, the conscious sensation produced is referred to the location of the receptor”. This is:
question.explanation: This statement describes the law of projection: sensation is perceived at the location of the receptor field served by the stimulated pathway, even if the pathway is activated elsewhere along its course.
question.keyConcept: The law of projection localizes sensation to the receptor field.
options: Muller’s law of specific nerve energies

question.text: Which of the following is a rapidly adapting sensory receptor?
question.explanation: Rapidly adapting receptors respond strongly to changes in stimulus intensity and are well represented by touch receptors such as Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles. Pain receptors and muscle spindles adapt more slowly.
question.keyConcept: Rapidly adapting receptors signal stimulus change, especially touch.

question.text: Which of the following does not apply to chemical synapses:
question.explanation: Opening chloride channels is generally inhibitory, not stimulatory, so that statement does not apply to chemical synapses. Chemical synapses do require calcium for release and can involve inhibitory transmitters and multiple inputs.
question.keyConcept: Chloride-channel opening is usually inhibitory, not stimulatory.
options: More than one neurotransmitter may be released
Neurotransmitter that opens Cl channels are stimulatory to postsynaptic neurons
Ca2+ is needed for the release of transmitter from presynaptic neurons
Activity of postsynaptic neuron is determined by many presynaptic neurons

question.text: The following is not a feature of chemical synapses:
question.explanation: Typical chemical synapses conduct in one direction from presynaptic to postsynaptic cell. Bidirectional transmission is instead a feature of many electrical synapses.
question.keyConcept: Chemical synapses are usually unidirectional.
options: Transmission of impulse in both directions

question.text: The following is needed for the normal functioning of a chemical synapse except:
question.explanation: Chemical synapses require transmitter, presynaptic calcium entry, postsynaptic receptors, and a mechanism to remove transmitter. Gap junctions are a feature of electrical synapses, not a normal requirement for chemical synapses.
question.keyConcept: Gap junctions are not required for chemical synapses.
options: Gap junctions between pre-synaptic and post-synaptic neurons
Ca++ channels in the synaptic knobs
A receptor for the neurotransmitter on the post-synaptic neuron
A removal mechanism for the neurotransmitter

question.text: An excitatory post-synaptic potential would develop if the neurotransmitter:
question.explanation: An excitatory postsynaptic potential develops when the transmitter causes net depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane. In this option set, opening calcium channels is the excitatory choice among the listed alternatives.
question.keyConcept: EPSPs arise from postsynaptic depolarization.

question.text: The transmission of impulses across chemical synapses may occur without the need for:
question.explanation: In immediate synaptic transmission, transmitter release, receptors, calcium, and a presynaptic action potential are essential. The Na+/K+ pump is crucial for long-term ionic homeostasis but is not the immediate special requirement for a single transmission event in this item.
question.keyConcept: A single synaptic event depends directly on release machinery more than on immediate pump action.

question.text: The excitatory postsynaptic potential:
question.explanation: An EPSP is a graded depolarization produced by neurotransmitter action on the postsynaptic membrane, usually through sodium entry. EPSPs can summate and help bring the membrane toward threshold, but they are not all-or-none.
question.keyConcept: EPSPs are graded depolarizations, usually driven by Na+ influx.
options: Is due to neurotransmitter release from pre-synaptic neurons

question.text: The receptor potential:
question.explanation: A receptor potential is graded rather than all-or-none, and its size varies with stimulus intensity. It is a local potential and is not itself a propagated action potential.
question.keyConcept: Receptor potentials are graded and depend on stimulus intensity.
options: Is decreased by increasing the frequency of stimulation
Is influenced by changing the intensity of stimulation

question.text: The Renshaw cell
question.explanation: Renshaw cells are inhibitory spinal interneurons activated by recurrent collaterals from alpha motor neurons. They feed back to inhibit neighboring or the same motor pools.
question.keyConcept: Renshaw cells mediate recurrent inhibition in the spinal cord.
options: receive recurrent collaterals from motor neurons and inhibit other motor neurons in the vicinity
is the inhibitory system of the cerebellum
are a major component of muscle spindle

question.text: The naked nerve endings are responsible for the sensation of
question.explanation: Free or naked nerve endings are important receptors for pain. More specialized encapsulated receptors are used for modalities such as vibration, fine touch, hearing, and vision.
question.keyConcept: Free nerve endings commonly mediate pain sensation.

question.text: Which part of a neuron contains the nucleus?
question.explanation: Synaptic transmission involves presynaptic neurotransmitter release, diffusion across the synaptic cleft, and postsynaptic receptor binding, producing either excitatory (EPSP) or inhibitory (IPSP) potentials.
question.keyConcept: Soma contains the neuron's nucleus.

question.text: How much of a change in the membrane potential is necessary for the summation of postsynaptic potentials to result in an action potential being generated?
question.explanation: About +15 mV depolarization (from -70 to -55 mV threshold) is needed for AP generation.
question.keyConcept: EPSP summation: ~+15 mV to reach threshold.

question.text: A channel opens on a postsynaptic membrane that causes a negative ion to enter the cell. What type of graded potential is this?
question.explanation: A negative ion entering the cell causes hyperpolarization (inhibitory graded potential).
question.keyConcept: Negative ion entry → hyperpolarization (IPSP).

question.text: What type of receptor requires an effector protein to initiate a signal?
question.explanation: A metabotropic receptor has no channel of its own. Binding activates an associated G protein, which then acts on an effector enzyme such as adenylate cyclase or phospholipase C to generate second messengers. This indirect route makes the response slower in onset but longer lasting and greatly amplified, in contrast to an ionotropic receptor, which is itself the ion channel and responds within milliseconds.
question.keyConcept: Ionotropic receptors are fast channels; metabotropic receptors are slow, amplified and G-protein coupled.

question.text: What type of receptor cell is responsible for transducing pain stimuli?
question.explanation: Painful stimuli are transduced by nociceptors, free nerve endings whose channels are opened by tissue-damaging mechanical, thermal and chemical energy and which signal centrally over thin myelinated A-delta and unmyelinated C fibres. Photoreceptors transduce light, mechanoreceptors transduce deformation, and osmoreceptors respond to changes in fluid osmolality.
question.keyConcept: Match each receptor class to the form of energy it transduces; nociceptors are the damage detectors.

question.text: What type of receptor cell is involved in the sensations of sound and balance?
question.explanation: Hearing and balance both depend on hair cells, which are mechanoreceptors. Deflection of their stereocilia opens mechanically gated ion channels and produces a receptor potential, so the physical energy of sound waves or of head movement is transduced into an electrical signal. The same cell type serves both senses, differing only in the accessory structures of cochlea and vestibular apparatus.
question.keyConcept: Hair cells transduce mechanical deflection into receptor potentials for both hearing and balance.

question.text: Which region of gray matter in the spinal cord contains motor neurons that innervate skeletal muscles?
question.explanation: The alpha motor neurons that innervate skeletal muscle lie in the ventral horn of the spinal grey matter, and their axons leave the cord in the ventral root. The dorsal horn is the sensory receiving area and the lateral horn houses preganglionic autonomic neurons. This division is why a ventral horn disease such as poliomyelitis causes pure flaccid weakness with wasting and no sensory loss.
question.keyConcept: Ventral horn is motor, dorsal horn sensory, lateral horn autonomic.

question.text: What type of reflex can protect the foot when a painful stimulus is sensed?
question.explanation: A painful stimulus to the foot evokes the flexor withdrawal reflex, a polysynaptic spinal reflex that flexes the limb away from the source of injury. Crossed extension of the opposite limb accompanies it so that body weight can still be supported. Because it is organised entirely within the cord, the movement begins before the stimulus is consciously perceived.
question.keyConcept: Flexor withdrawal is a protective polysynaptic spinal reflex, faster than conscious perception.

question.text: Which of the following represents a sensory input that is not part of both the somatic and autonomic systems?
question.explanation: Baroreceptor input from the carotid sinus and aortic arch never reaches consciousness and feeds only autonomic reflex arcs that adjust heart rate and vascular tone. Vision, taste and proprioception all reach the cerebral cortex and are consciously perceived, so they serve somatic sensation even though they can also trigger autonomic responses.
question.keyConcept: Autonomic afferents such as baroreceptors drive reflexes without ever reaching consciousness.

question.text: What is the term for a reflex that does not include a CNS component?
question.explanation: A short reflex is completed entirely within the peripheral plexuses, so the sensory neuron, interneuron and motor neuron all lie in the enteric nervous system of the gut wall and no signal ever reaches the brain or spinal cord. This local autonomy is why an isolated segment of intestine still shows coordinated peristalsis. Long reflexes, by contrast, route through the central nervous system.
question.keyConcept: Short reflexes are completed in the enteric plexuses, while long reflexes pass through the CNS.

question.text: A drug is called an agonist if it does which of the following?
question.explanation: An agonist binds a receptor and activates it, reproducing the effect of the natural transmitter, whereas an antagonist binds without activating and merely prevents the natural transmitter from acting. Agonists are further graded by efficacy, since a full agonist produces the maximal response and a partial agonist a submaximal one even when every receptor is occupied.
question.keyConcept: Agonists bind and activate; antagonists bind and block without activating.
options: acts like the endogenous neurotransmitter by binding to its receptor
blocks the voltage-gated calcium ion channel

question.text: Which of the following discharge spontaneously during quiet breathing
question.explanation: The dorsal respiratory group in the medulla contains the inspiratory neurons that generate the basic rhythm, firing in spontaneous ramped bursts that set the pace of quiet breathing. Motor neurons of the respiratory muscles are driven rather than autorhythmic, lung stretch receptors respond only when the lung inflates, and the ventral group is largely silent in quiet breathing and is recruited only when forced expiration is needed.
question.keyConcept: The dorsal respiratory group is the intrinsic rhythm generator; the ventral group serves forced breathing.

question.text: Hering-Breuer inflation reflex in human being
question.explanation: The inflation reflex is a protective brake rather than a routine control.
